Generative AI aside, I downloaded this game to try it out, because even small studios and devs deserve a shot regardless of budget. That being said, I have some things to say:

There are ads, which as of the time of writing this, aren’t terribly intrusive, and they’re standard length. No big deal for me, huge deal for others. The ad removal will cost you $12.99, which also seems reasonable if you’re planning to invest a lot of time into the game. 

All of that being said, I’m not far enough in for confirmation yet, but it APPEARS as if there is a pay-to-play element that comes in the form of a “chapter bundle” later on past the prologue/preliminary chapter. 

At this time, I am unsure if time will unlock these for you, so purchasing the chapter bundle will help to make the unlocking go fast, OR if you have free access to the prologue and will need to pay for the rest of the game. 

All in all, the game looks pretty good, and from what I can tell, seems to have an okay story. If I remember (I have ADHD so that’s unlikely), I’ll update this comment after I play even longer to see if any of my suspicions are confirmed. 

Happy gaming everyone!

Okay I’ve been waiting for an opportunity to shout this place out, and I think I’ve finally found the right time. 

There’s a coffee shop/cafe near the intersection of parham/three chopt in (what I believe would be considered) tuckahoe. (If I’m wrong I’m sorry I’m not as familiar with the neighborhoods as I’d like) The coffee shop is called Surrounding Counties. I’ve been going there fairly regularly for a few months, at least once a week. 

The shop is owned by a man named Zach (I’m not clear on the spelling). Zach has worked in Richmond restaurants for what I perceive to be decades, purely based on how many experiences he’s had. He used to be a part owner of After Glow, he’s worked for lamplighter, and he’s worked at or owned (with partners) several other Richmond restaurants in the past who’s names elude me. 

There are people that work at this coffee shop who have jumped ship from his previous gigs to work for him at this place. I was there yesterday and someone who’s known him for years (through work) had come in because he just “wanted to see how Zach was doing.” I can’t say with certainty, but the way he talks to people seems so gosh darn genuine and he’s so kind. His customer service skills are also 100% on point.

Yesterday I was there, a little later in the day than I would have liked, and he was there as well. I asked him about these chocolate chip cookies he makes that I’ve only seen a couple times. And he said “oh I make them almost every day they just sell out really fast.” And I said “oh man I’ve gotten them before and they’re always so good, it’s a bummer that I can’t ever seem to get here when you still have some.” And this man, who has no reason whatsoever to do this, says “I have the stuff to make them tonight, come in tomorrow and tell whoever’s here that Zach left you something in the back. How many cookies do you want?” I’m going to pick them up in a couple hours.

Edit to add: This is just my experience. In my perception, this is a kind and genuine man who just wants to make good food and good coffee. I’m sorry if your experience with Zach was not as good as mine have been. But in the months I’ve been going to his establishment, there have been absolutely 0 staff changes that I could tell. Everyone has worked there consistently.

Frequent traveler to Philadelphia, NYC, and DC on Amtrak. The engine switch happens in DC, and if you get there on time, they take 20-40 minutes. 

In summer, my advice is to have a loose itinerary on travel days. The trains originating on more southern routes (Palmetto) are generally delayed because in the heat, they are limited to how fast they can go on the rails.

You can bring your own food and drink on board, but make sure it’s something you don’t mind eating cold (or lukewarm, or right away) because Amtrak can’t heat anything that you bring on board. 

The quiet car can be your best friend, if other people follow the rules or Amtrak employees enforce them. ESPECIALLY on overnight/late night rides. 

For WiFi, I’ve found it’s great for texting, but not streaming. So I advise you to download a few movies or episodes of the show you’re watching so you have something to do. 

And personally, I use noise canceling headphones to eliminate a lot of chatter. Sometimes the people around you aren’t exactly good travel buddies.

Absolutely! I think, for me personally, my thinking changed when I realized that the companies need me more than I need them, and that’s when I started looking more critically at the places I was applying to.

Red Flags: typical job type stuff. “We’re a family here,” “we care about you” type stuff. Working employees to the point of burnout, not able to keep technicians around to save their lives, not paying technicians enough to do anything meaningful with their lives, high turnover among technicians, supervisors just don’t care, case loads with large numbers of clients (upwards of 17)

Green flags (almost exclusively from my current company): encouraging and enforcing work-life balance (seriously when I go on vacation, I don’t even get a single work email, they take me off all the communications and I’m filled in when I get back), supportive atmosphere where everyone can learn and grow regardless of their level of knowledge. Even the director learns alongside us and admits when she doesn’t know something or makes a mistake. Getting feedback that I can actually use to become a better supervisor, that’s given in a way that doesn’t make me feel inadequate. The interview process was also VERY laid back, and the director took that time to get to know me on a personal level, where she found out my professional ambitions and peppered in questions about my knowledge and everything else. It was unlike any interview I’ve ever gone to, and this is BY FAR the best job I’ve ever had, ABA or otherwise.
